content:
A utility helicopter needs to be described through the work it performs, not merely its model and value. Different activities can change the questions concerning the aircraft, people, equipment and liability. For a company in the Republic of Moldova, an insurance review starts with an inventory of operations and contractual relationships. The general description “aerial services” is not sufficient.

This article helps prepare an assessment file. It does not confirm that a solution is available for a particular helicopter or special operation. The Civil Aviation Authority publishes information on insurance in air transport, while the local insurer consulted presents Aero-Casco and aviation liability separately. Actual conditions, legal requirements and acceptance of the activity require individual review. This text contains no flight, emergency response or work execution procedures.

Start with the service, then the aircraft

Prepare a list of activities actually planned and customer organisation types, without unnecessary personal information. Distinguish repositioning the aircraft from the service performed at the destination. A transport description should not replace the description of utility work. Name any special activities clearly and submit them for assessment without assuming they will be accepted.

For each service type, record the area, period, contracting parties and relevant equipment. Do not declare a narrower activity to simplify assessment. A new operation needs to be disclosed before existing documents are considered sufficient. The fact that the helicopter and team remain the same does not automatically establish identical conditions for different work.

Who owns, operates and contracts the work?

The aircraft owner may differ from the operator and the business signing the commercial contract. Prepare a simple map of these relationships with the entities' exact names. State whether financing, rental or another right of use exists. A useful assessment must identify each party's interest, not only the person paying the premium.

The customer's contract may contain insurance requirements or assumed obligations. These need legal review and comparison with the proposed insurance documents. Do not assume that every responsibility promised commercially is insurable or accepted. A short certificate does not resolve differences between the commercial description and the activity the insurer has actually assessed.

The aircraft profile must be current

Identify the helicopter using its documents and describe the relevant configuration. Distinguish installed equipment from detachable equipment and assets belonging to other organisations. Where modifications exist, retain the relevant technical records and identify a competent person who can explain them. The broker does not certify the configuration or decide whether work can be performed safely.

Do not rely solely on a photograph or a manufacturer's brochure. Prepare identification of the actual asset, its valuation basis and documents requested through the agreed channel. Supply detailed technical information only when needed. Do not publish serial numbers, work plans or sensitive information in a publicly accessible form simply to request an indicative price.

The aircraft itself and liability are separate questions

For the aircraft, ask how the insured object and relevant events are defined in the Aero-Casco document. For liability, ask which insured persons, activities and categories of claims are under discussion. Do not assume either assessment automatically includes the other or that a shared aviation insurance heading resolves every question.

Distinguish the company's staff, people transported, property and third parties in the work area. Their treatment needs explanation using the actual documents. Legal obligations, amounts and operating conditions require specialist review at the time of the decision. This article establishes none of those requirements and does not automatically apply foreign rules to a Moldovan company.

Utility equipment needs a separate inventory

A job may depend on equipment outside the usual configuration described in a previous assessment. Prepare its inventory, owner, value and contractual relationship. Do not assume an accessory is included simply because it is used with the aircraft. Ask how it is treated at each relevant stage without publishing installation or operating instructions.

If equipment is rented or belongs to the customer, distinguish damage to the item from contractual liability. Retain handover records and condition observations completed by competent people. A good inventory helps identification but does not guarantee acceptance of a value or risk. Any conclusion concerning protection must be traceable to the conditions of the document under review.

Sites and changes to the project

Describe operating areas and project stages at the level needed for assessment, without disclosing details that could compromise operational security. A site change may affect relationships with the customer, third parties and contractors. Do not assume a policy for a previous project automatically covers another contract using the same aircraft.

Use a change record showing the original information, proposed change and response received. Where the project involves other jurisdictions, check their requirements separately with appropriate specialists. Policy territory and permission to perform the work are distinct questions. An answer to one must not be presented as an answer to the other.

Values, costs and business continuity

Document aircraft value, equipment and project expenses separately. The cost of an unperformed contract is not automatically damage to the aircraft. A period without income or a commercial penalty should not be added to the asset's value without checking. Ask which components could be considered for insurance and on what basis, without promising that one policy protects every financial consequence.

For continuity planning, the company can document reliance on equipment and contractors while keeping operational analysis separate from insurance. An alternative plan does not confirm lost-income cover, and insurance does not replace planning. Financial data, contracts and other commercial information should be supplied in a controlled manner only to people legitimately involved in the assessment.

What should be checked before accepting a proposal?

Read the entity names, aircraft identification, use and equipment. Check the periods and areas described, exclusions and special conditions. Exclusions are situations not covered, while the deductible is the part of the loss borne under the contract. Ask about separate limits and any conditions concerning special activities instead of assuming standard wording is sufficient.

The insurance premium is the amount paid for the policy. Compare proposals only for the same activities and values. A price difference may reflect a different scope rather than a saving for identical protection. The broker can support clarification within its mandate, but the insurer accepts the risk and examines compensation under the contract.

Incident documentation must not be improvised

Technical, safety and authority reporting procedures are established with competent specialists. For insurance, retain the notification instructions and contacts stated in the actual document. Do not borrow deadlines from motor insurance or assume an informal commercial message replaces the notification required by the contract.

Depending on the incident and file requirements, relevant records may concern the chronology, people and assets involved. Do not retrospectively alter records to fit a conclusion. If an event is already known, describe it confidentially and request assessment of the applicable documents. Future insurance must not be presented as an automatic remedy for that event.

Example of assessing a new job

In a hypothetical scenario, an operator receives a request for a service different from the one described in its previous file. It prepares a job profile, the entities involved and equipment, rather than assuming the same helicopter's name is sufficient. This example does not describe an ING Broker customer or confirm an operation's eligibility.

Instead of sending only the contract value, the company separates questions concerning the aircraft, equipment, third parties and commercial obligations. Unresolved points remain visible until an answer is received. This administrative organisation helps avoid unjustified promises to the customer, but it does not replace the project's technical, legal and operational review.

A short preparation checklist

  • The entities and their roles in ownership or operation.
  • Actual services and changes from previously assessed activities.
  • Aircraft identification and documented configuration.
  • Equipment, owners and substantiated values.
  • Areas, periods and relationships with the customer.
  • Contractual requirements and points needing specialist review.
  • Written responses and limits still unconfirmed.

A matrix for equipment, work and customer relationships

For a programme involving several services, a matrix can list jobs in rows and aircraft, equipment, owners and relevant contracts in columns. It is an administrative record, not an operational procedure. It shows where the same component is used in a different context and where an accessory belongs to the customer rather than the operator. These differences can then be submitted for assessment without ambiguous descriptions.

For each combination, record whether a documented answer exists, clarification has been requested or information is unavailable. Do not turn an unanswered question into confirmation. A project profile may remain incomplete until a competent person checks the technical document or contractual relationship. Keeping an issue open is more accurate than reproducing conditions from different work.

Update the matrix for a new contract before making an insurance statement to the customer. This allows the commercial description, inventory and assessed documents to be traced together without suggesting that an administrative record authorises the operation or confirms its safety.

Frequently asked questions about utility helicopters

Does a transport policy include all utility work?

Do not assume so. The actual activity must be declared and checked. The general name of the aircraft or its services does not establish acceptance of a special operation.

Is rented equipment included with the aircraft?

Not automatically. Identify the owner, value, use and handover documents. Ask for the asset and obligations towards its owner to be assessed separately.

Does the customer's contract establish policy cover?

No. The commercial contract and insurance conditions are different documents. Customer requirements must be analysed and compared with the protection actually confirmed, without promising that every obligation is included.

What should I check for a new utility job?

Describe the service, customer, aircraft and equipment, then request verification of insurance documents for that activity. Do not automatically transfer an answer received for transport or a previous project. Authorisation, safety and technical requirements must be checked separately with competent people. A policy does not authorise the work.

Next step

Request a discussion with ING Broker to explore possibilities for assessment and intermediation. The broker explains options and facilitates the process. The insurer accepts the risk, determines conditions and handles claims under the contract. This guide confirms neither product availability nor cover for an individual case.
